questions.q: Let $A$~be the point  \left(1, 2\right)$~and $B$ be any point on the curve $x^{2} + y^{2} = 16$. If the centre of the locus of the point $P$, which divides the line segment $AB$~in the ratio $3: 2$~is the point $C \left(\alpha, \beta\right), then the length of the line segment $AC& is$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$A$~be the point \left(1, 2\right)$~and $B$ be any point on the curve $x^{2} + y^{2} = 16$,

And the centre of the locus of the point $P$, which divides the line segment $AB$~in the ratio $3: 2$~is the point $C \left(\alpha, \beta\right),

Now let the point on the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} = 16$~be~$B \left(4cos\theta, 4sin\theta\right)$

Now using section formula in~$A \left(1, 2\right)$~and~$B \lleft(4cos\theta,4sin\theta)$~we get,

P \left(\dfrac{12cos\theta + 2}{5}, \dfrac{12sin\theta + 4}{5}\right)$≡ ( h, k )$

$⇒ $cos\theta = \dfrac{5h - 2}{12}$ \text{ and } $sin\theta = \dfrac{5k - 4}{12}

Now squaring and adding we get,

\left(\dfrac{5h - 2}{12})$2 + \left(\dfrac{5k - 4}{12}\right)2 = 1$

$⇒ \left(h - \dfrac{2}{5}\right)2 + \left($k - $\dfrac{4}{5}\right)$2 = \left(\dfrac{12}{5}\right)2$

So, the centre of the locus is~$C\left(\dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{4}{5}\right)$

Hence, by distance formula we get,$AC = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{6}{5}\right)2} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}$

$

questions.q: Let the locus of the mid points of the chords of circle $x^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)2 = 1$ drawn from the origin intersect the line $x + y = 1$ at $P$ and $Q$. Then, the length of $PQ$ is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let the mid point of the chords be \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$.

The given equation of circle is $x^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)2 = 1$.

$⇒ x^{2} + y^{2} - 2y = 0$

$⇒ x{x}_{1} + y{y}_{1} - \left(y + {y}_{1}\right) = {x1}^{2} + {y1}^{2} - 2{y}_{1}$

This locus passes through the origin,

$⇒ 0 + 0 - \left(0 + {y}_{1}\right) = {x1}^{2} + {y1}^{2} - 2{y}_{1}$

$⇒ - {y}_{1} = {x1}^{2} + {y1}^{2} - 2{y}_{1}$

$⇒ {x1}^{2} + {y1}^{2} - {y}_{1} = 0$

So, the locus is $x^{2} + y^{2} - y = 0$

It intersects with the line $x + y = 1$.

$⇒ \left(1 - y\right)2 + y^{2} - y = 0$

$⇒ 1 + y^{2} - 2y + y^{2} - y = 0$

$⇒ 2y^{2} - 2y - y + 1 = 0$

$⇒ 2y\left(y - 1\right) - \left(y - 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(2y - 1\right) \left($y - 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ y = 1, $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ P ≡ \left(0, 1\right)\text{and}Q \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)

$⇒ PQ = $\sqrt{\left(0 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)2 + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}

$⇒ PQ = $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4}}

$⇒ PQ = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$

questions.q: Let the abscissae of the two points& $P$~and~$Q$~on a circle be the roots of~$x^{2} - 4x - 6 = 0$~and the ordinates of~$P$~and~$Q$~be the roots of~$y^{2} + 2y - 7 = 0$. If~$PQ$~is a diameter of the circle~$x^{2} + y^{2} + 2ax + 2by + c = 0$, then the value of~  \left(a + b - c\right)$& is$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given that the roots of $x^{2} - 4x - 6 = 0$~are the abscissa~of the end of diameter

i.e.~${x}_{1} + {x}_{2} = 4, {x}_{1}{x}_{2} = - 6$

and roots of $y^{2} + 2y - 7 = 0$~are ordinate of the end of diameter

i.e.~${y}_{1} + {y}_{2} = - 2, {y}_{1}{y}_{2} = - 7$

Now, equation of the circle will be

\left(x - {x}_{1}\right)\left(x - {x}_{2}\right) + \left(y - {y}_{1}\right)\left(y - {y}_{2}\right) = 0$

i.e.~$x^{2} - \left({x}_{1} + {x}_{2}\right)x + {x}_{1}{x}_{2} + y^{2} - \left({y}_{1} + {y}_{2}\right)y + {y}_{1}{y}_{2} = 0$

$⇒ x^{2} + y^{2} - 4x + 2y - 13 = 0$

$∴ a = - 2, b = 1, c = - 13$

$⇒ a + b - c = - 2 + 1 + 13 = 12$

$

questions.q: Let the circle& $S: 36x^{2} + 36y^{2} - 108x + 120y + C = 0$~be such that it neither intersects nor touches the co-ordinate axes. If the point of intersection of the lines, $x - 2y = 4$~and $2x - y = 5$ lies inside the circle $S,$ then:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The given circle is& $S: 36x^{2} + 36y^{2} - 108x + 120y + C = 0$

$⇒ x^{2} + y^{2} - 3x + \dfrac{10}{3}y + \dfrac{C}{36} = 0$

We know that the centre and radius of a circle~$x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$~is~ \left(- g, - f\right)$~and~$\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}$~respectively.

Thus, centre~$e ≡ \left(-g, - f\right) ≡ \left(\dfrac{3}{2}, - \dfrac{10}{6}\right)~and~radius~$= r = $\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{100}{36} - \dfrac{C}{36}}

Now, this circle neither intersects nor touches the co-ordinate axes, hence, the radius of the circle is less than the absolute value of the co-ordinate with smaller value.

$⇒ r < \dfrac{3}{2}$

$\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{100}{36} - \dfrac{C}{36}} < \dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{100}{36} - \dfrac{C}{36} < \dfrac{9}{4}$

$⇒ C > 100 \ldots \left(1\right)$

Now, point of intersection of $x - 2y = 4$~and $2x - y = 5$~is $( 2, - 1 ) ,$~which lies inside the circle $S .$

The point~ \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$~lies inside a circle~$x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0,$~if~${x}_{1}^{2} + {y}_{1}^{2} + 2g{x}_{1} + 2f{y}_{1} + c < 0$

$⇒ \left(2\right)2 + \left(- 1\right)2 - 3\left(2\right) + \dfrac{10}{3}\left(- 1\right) + \dfrac{C}{36} < 0$

$⇒ 4 + 1 - 6 - \dfrac{10}{3} + \dfrac{C}{36} < 0$

$⇒ C < 156 \ldots \left(2\right)$

From \left(1\right)$~and \left(2\right),$~we have~$100 < C < 156$

$

questions.q: A line segment $AB$ of length~$\lambda$ moves such that the points $A$ and $B$ remain on the periphery of a circle of radius $\lambda$. Then the locus of the point, that divides the line segment $AB$ in the ratio $2: 3$, is a circle of radius
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$

Given,

A line segment $AB$ of length~$\lambda$ moves such that the points $A$ and $B$ remain on the periphery of a circle of radius $\lambda$,

Now taking the points on the circle of radius~$\lambda$~as~$B\left(\lambda cos{θ}_{1}, \lambda sin{θ}_{1}\right) \text{ and } A \left(\lambda cos{θ}_{2}\lambda sin{θ}_{2}\right)$~and taking the point~$P \left(h, k\right)$~which divides the line segment in~$AB$~of length~$\lambda$~in~$2: 3$

Now plotting the diagram we get,

Now, let $O$ be the origin and radius of circle is~$\lambda$ and ~$AB = \lambda$~and using distance formula we get,

$AB = \lambda = \sqrt{\left(\lambda cos{θ}_{1} - \lambda cos{θ}_{2}\right)2 + \left(\lambda sin{θ}_{1} - \lambda sin{θ}_{2}\right)2}$

$⇒ 1 = 2 - 2\cos \left({θ}_{1} - {θ}_{2}\right)

$⇒ $\cos \left({θ}_{1} - {θ}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}

Now using section formula we get,

$h = $\dfrac{2\lambda cos{θ}_{1} + 3\lambda cos{θ}_{2}}{5}~and $k = $\dfrac{2\lambda sin{θ}_{1} + 3\lambda sin{θ}_{2}}{5}

Now squaring and adding above two value we get,

$h^{2} + k^{2} = $\dfrac{\lambda2}{25} \left[$4 + 9 + 12 \left($\cos \left({θ}_{1} - {θ}_{2}\right)\right)\right]$

$⇒ h^{2} + k^{2} = $\dfrac{\lambda2}{25} \cdot$19$

Hence, Radius~$= \dfrac{λ}{5}\sqrt{19}$

$
